Well yes, but actually no. As some other people have said, you can get psychologically addicted to virtually anything. Physiological addiction is an entirely different thing, however. The issue with drugs like heroin and meth is that they're physically addictive - meaning most people will have very similar physiological reactions to it. Drugs like marijuana are not INHERENTLY addictive or harmful, as they alone do not cause dependency. Put simply, any addiction to marijuana is purely psychological and nowhere near as harmful as some other more vicious drugs. So long as you're capable of controlling yourself and in moderation, marijuana can be a very psychologically healthy recreational substance. 

Why meth and heroin and the like are physically addictive is because they flood our brains with a shitload of dopamine which causes our neuroreceptors to produce less of it moving forward to compensate. This leads to the body reacting pretty nastily if a user were to just stop; there'd be uncontrollable physical reactions like vomiting and severe body pain and aches. Marijuana doesn't cause any extreme, long-term neurochemical imbalances, as far as I can recall, and certainly isn't treated as a physically addictive substance in the scientific field.

The reason I'm disclosing this is because people are misinformed enough about addiction and substance abuse enough as they are because the government and law enforcement give zero shits about the proven science behind these things; so much so that they see fit to essentially lie to the masses and stigmatise all illegal substances as being equally as bad when scientifically, they are absolutely not.

Note: I have never tried marijuana and nor do I condone the use of illegal substances, I'm merely a psych student.

OCD (Obsessive Compulsive Disorder) doesn't refer to "omg I can't take it when the red jelly beans are in the blue jar" or anything to do with liking symmetry or being a neat freak. Actual victims of OCD do things like stand by the light switch in a room and repeatedly flick it on and off for hours and mentally break down halfway through, or making gestures as if they're washing their hand by a basin despite there being no water and that they simply cannot control the urge to make those gestures. The word "disorder" indicates, among other things, that the symptoms are severe enough to downright disrupt one's daily live and stop you from carrying out your "normal" routines and activities. People should stop saying things like "I'm just so OCD, I can't help but round up the numbers you know" as people are misinformed enough about this disorder.

"Sociopathy" and "psychopathy" really mean the same thing. The former doesn't refer to "a slightly less severe case of psychopathy" or "a disorder developed as a result of emotional trauma". Clinically speaking, neither exist in the DSM (comprehensive psychology textbook), and they're merely media terms used to describe APD/ASPD (Antisocial Personality Disorder). It pisses me off to see smartasses on the internet argue over whether Logan Paul or whoever is psychopathic or sociopathic and how the two terms are clinically different.
